Introductory
THE Publishers take pleasure in presenting herewilh the Twenty-ninth Annual
E>d;ition of Henderson's Vancouver Directory, embracing the area of Greater
Vancouver and compiising the city proper, South Vancouver. Point Grey,
Burnaby (part), Richmond (part), Xorth Vancouver City, District of Xorth Van-
couver and West Vancouv<?r.
Numerous ahtanges of address were recorded after the Street Dii-ectory was
printed, and in such cases the name of the householder on the sti-eet will differ
from name in tihe Alphabetical Section. The latter being the latest information,
should be taken as the more correct.
The Advertising D-epartment presents the names of corporations, firms and
individuals who have made Vancouver the great city that it is, and who are
a power in the financial, industrial and commercial world of Western Canada.
The Classified Directory contains a complete alphabetically arranged list of
the various trades and profes.si1ons carried on in Vancouver. This will be found
useful for reference and a most efficient buyer's guide.
Tihe Miscellaneous Section in the front of this volume contains information
about the public officials and institutions of the City and adjoining Municipalities,
also Churches, Societies and Associations, much of which is not to be found else-
where  in print.
The value of the Street Section is not apprecSiated perhaps, to the extent it
sliould be by some wlio desire to find a certain house on a street unfamiliar to
them.
By application of the following exan\ple the location of any street number
can be found expeditiously: Suppose 428 Georgia Street is wanted: refer to street
section Georgia Street — glance down to 42cS. then to the nearest intersection to 428.
It will be found that this number is on the south .side of the street, three houses
east of Homer, between Homer and Richards Streets.
The Vancouver Directory is placed in Directory and Public Libraries and other
institutions throughout Canada and the United States, where it serves the public
as a valuable book of reference. It also constitutes a splendid and unrivalled
standing advertisement for the city it represents, as no other publication can
convey such an adequate idea of the city, its varied business interests and its
different institutions and organizations. Few people realize what a wide and
unique publicity tWis affords the city and its industries.

WATER WORKS
Water works are owned by the Muni-
cipality. The source of supply is the
mountain s^treams known as Capilano
Creek and Seymour Creek, which are
dammed across at an elevation of 580
feet above sea level, about 8 miles north
of the city. The average height of the
city is about 100 feet, the extreme
height south of False Creek (Mt. Pleas-
ant) being 200 feet. A reservoir of
24,000,000 gallons capacity is situated at
Little Mountain at an elevation of 395
feet above the extreme high water
mark, and adds much to the efficiency
and security of the system, and nor-
mally takes care of the supply to the
high level districts. There are approxi-
mately 267 miles of distribution mains
in the city.

Burnaby Municipality
(Incorporated 1892)
Burnaby Municipality occupies the
height of land between Vancouver on
the west and Xew Westminster on the
east. It fronts on the north arm of
Fraser River on the south and on Bur-
rard Inlet on the north, and its total
area is 38 square miles. It has the
advantages of both fresh and salt water
harbour facilities with direct access to
the sea. Its harbour frontage comprises
twelve miles.
The district being conveniently situate
between the cities of Vancouver and
New Westminster, is becoming rapidly
popular as a residential district, espec-
ially along the ridges in the north and
in the south. The lower lands are suit-
able for market gardening, and the rais-
ing of small fruits, which is a growing
industry, and there are several lumber
and shingle mills operating in the muni-
cipality.
The district has a system of excellent
roads, including some S^ miles of
paved highways, and approximately 30
miles of macadamized highways. The
municipality possesses its own water
.system, drawing its supply from Seymour
Creek, and is in a position to furnish
water at cheap rates. The district is
well served by railways, having two
steam roads and three electric roads
running through from east to west.
Every portion of .the municipality is
within easy access of excellent schools,
and the electric light and telephone is
available through the greater portions
of the municipality.

City of North Vancouver
The City of North Vancouver occupies
an ideal location on the north shore of
Burrard Inlet, directly opposite the city
of Vancouver, from which it is distant
about two and one-quarter miles, and
with which it is connected by means of
a modern ferry service operated on a
twenty-minute schedule.
The «^ntire north shore of the Inlet
originally comprised the district muni-
cipality of North Vancouver, but a cen-
tre of population having sprung up at
the most convenient point, the city was
incorporated on May 13th. 1907. the
boundaries enclosing about 4.000 acres.
The townsite is of the highest excel-
lence in every respect. For a distance
of twenty miles the north shore of Bur-
rard Inlet offers an unbroken water-
front, available for shipping and indus-
trial purpo.ses. the greater portion of
which has sufficient depth of water for
the accommodation of ocean-going craft
of the deepest draft. Extensive tide
flats likewise ^xist. nroviding ideal
facilities for railway terminals, ware-
hou.«e. docking and other purposes.
The land rises from the seaboard on
about a three per cent, grade, creatine
the v,^.<t natural conditions for sewage
and drainage, and likewise providing an
elevation which affords an excellent
vi^>w from all parts of the townsite.
which constitutes one of the greatest
attractions from a residential stand-
po'nt. The slope is toward the soutn.
wh'l^^ toward the north the location is
protected by retreating hills, giving at
once a delightful combination of a sunny
southern slope effectively protected from
cold winds. The thoroughfares of the
city are wide, many being eighty feet,
and i^ome one hundred and one hundred
and fifty feet in width. There are in all
about one hundred acres w'thin the city
which have been .set aside for public
park purposes .the total of which is
swelled to 160 acres by including the
Grand Boulevard. 34 6 feet wide and
twelve blocks In length, a feature which
is distinctive and of the highest value
as the city Increases in population.
The environs of the city offer scenic
attractions which are seldom equalled.
The famous Capllano Canyon is a mar-
vel to even world-wide tourists, and is
within six miles of the city, with an
excellent roadway the entire distance
and street car service to within a mile.
The Canyon View Hotel offers excellent
accommodation here for tourists. Lynn
Canyon and Seymour Canyon are alike
grand and imposing and easily reached
by street car. Mountain climbing facili-
ties of the moderate order for the
amateur, or of the perilous for the more
venturesome, may be had within a few-
hours walk of the city
The telephone system of the B. C
Telephone Company gives modern local
and long distance facilities. The Pacific
Great Eastern Ry. runs trains everj- hour
Softener on Sundays and holidays) to
Whytecliffe (Horse Shoe Bay), a de-
llgTitful summer resort 13 miles north-
west: it is planned to continue this line
to Squamlsh when finances are more
favorable and join up with the main line
to Fort George, now in course of con-
struction. The water wDrks system is
owned by the corporation and was In-
stalled at a cost of $50,000. Large addi-
tional expenditures have slnco been
made. The system provides an un-
limited supply of the purest and coldest
glacier water. The domestic pressure is
regulated from 75 to 50 pounds, wTiich
admits of Increase to 260 pounds for
fire protection purposes.

The district was first surveved in
1907. On March 12. 1912, the letters
patent were issued for its incorporation.
The reeve and council were elected on
April 6. West Vancouver took its place
with its sister rtHinicipali-ty In the mak-
ing of Vancouver.
Less than twelve years have passed
since this great tract lying west of
CJapilano River was almost as wild as
it was five hundred years ago. When
it was first surveyed the district became
known as West Capilano. When it was
put on the market later it became known
SLS West Vancouver, and was incorpor-
ated under that name. For many years
the district was traversed only by Keitii
Road, which follows the sea westward.
In many places this was little more
than a trail, which could scarce be dis-
cerned in the woods. In 1910 the Gov-
ernment opened several roads, and
this work has been continued until at
the present time there are many miles
of roadway in West Vancouver, care-
fully graded.
Areas have been reserved for parks
and gardens, and the district is being
laid out with care to avoid anv un-
desirable features.
West Vancouver is divided into a
number of temporary centres of activ-
ity. Caulfeild. at the extreme west end.
is a summer resort. Horseshoe Bav is
noted as a summer bathing beach, 'ex-
press canyon and waterfall are within
tne boundaries.
One of the district's greatest assets is
the Point Atkinson Reserve now known
as Lighthouse Park. This promontory,
upon which stands the Point Atkinson
Lighthouse at the entrance of Howe
Sound. conta.ins ISO acres of diversified
dell and woodland, and needs only the
cutting of paths through it to make it
as attractive a holiday resort as can be
found on the shores of the Gulf of
Georgia.

Richmond Municipality
Municipal Hall, Brighouse, Lulu Island
Richmond Municipality lies south of
the Fraser River from Marpole. and
includes Lulu and Sea. Islands, both
highly intensified farming areas both
for grain growing and garden truck
production. Splendid breeds of horses
and cattle are raised also. The Munici-
pality is well served by ithe B. C E. Ry.
which runs to Steveston, the headquar-
ters    of the salmon fisheries at the
mouth of the Fraser Riv^r. Long dis-
tance telephone and electric light serve
l>ractically the whole district, which is
traversed by well kept highways.
